sections.heading: Patient Profile
sections.text:
The patient is a 76-year-old man, height 168 cm, weight 61 kg (BMI 21.6), with an unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg over the past 8 months. He lives with his spouse; his daughter, who lives nearby, is the primary family contact. He is independent for basic activities but needs assistance with shopping and stairs. He is a retired school teacher. He is an ex-smoker (30 pack-years, quit 12 years ago) and does not drink alcohol.

The patient has stated: "I want to be able to walk to the temple again and see my granddaughter's wedding next year. I will accept surgery if the doctors believe it is the right thing, but I am afraid of ending up on dialysis." His daughter has expressed concern about surgical risk and has asked whether "the valve can be fixed without open surgery."

sections.heading: Diagnoses and History
sections.text:
The patient presented to the cardiology outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness, now NYHA Class III (symptomatic walking approximately 100 metres or one flight of stairs), two episodes of exertional chest tightness, and one witnessed syncopal episode three weeks ago while climbing stairs, resulting in a minor fall without fracture.

Evaluation has confirmed severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with concomitant single-vessel coronary artery disease. The syncopal episode and worsening functional class indicate the disease has entered a high-risk symptomatic phase. Without intervention, symptomatic severe aortic stenosis of this profile carries a substantially elevated 1 to 2 year mortality risk.

sections.heading: Comorbidities
sections.text:
1. Chronic kidney disease, stage 3b — baseline creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m², stable over the last 12 months; followed by nephrology; no prior dialysis.
2. Type 2 diabetes mellitus — 18 years, on oral agents; HbA1c 7.8%; background diabetic retinopathy; likely contributor to nephropathy.
3. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (moderate) — FEV1 55% predicted; one exacerbation requiring oral steroids in the past year; on inhaled bronchodilator therapy; no home oxygen.
4. Prior transient ischaemic attack — 3 years ago, full recovery; carotid Doppler shows 50% right internal carotid stenosis, asymptomatic since.
5. Hypertension — controlled on two agents.
6. Mild chronic anaemia — haemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, attributed to chronic kidney disease; iron studies borderline.
7. Borderline frailty — Clinical Frailty Scale 4 to 5 (vulnerable to mildly frail); gait speed 0.7 m/s, which is slow; hand-grip strength below age norm; unintentional weight loss as noted in the patient profile. Cognition is intact, MoCA 26 out of 30. Mood is mildly anxious about surgery, with no depression.

sections.heading: Medications
sections.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily, dose-reduced for renal function. Gliclazide 40 mg once daily. Amlodipine 5 mg once daily. Telmisartan 40 mg once daily. Aspirin 75 mg once daily. Atorvastatin 40 mg at night. Tiotropium inhaler once daily; salbutamol inhaler as needed. Oral iron supplementation.

sections.heading: Allergies
sections.text: Documented allergy to iodinated contrast media — a previous moderate reaction of urticaria and bronchospasm during a CT scan 5 years ago, managed without intensive care. A premedication protocol is required for any contrast exposure. No known drug allergies otherwise.

sections.heading: Tests and Imaging
sections.text:
Laboratory results, 10 July: creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (reference 0.7 to 1.3), stable over 12 months. eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m² (reference above 90), consistent with chronic kidney disease stage 3b. Urea 58 mg/dL (reference 15 to 40), elevated. Potassium 4.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5 to 5.1), upper normal. Haemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (reference 13 to 17), mild anaemia. HbA1c 7.8% (reference below 6.5), suboptimal control. NT-proBNP 2450 pg/mL (reference below 300), significantly elevated. Albumin 3.4 g/dL (reference 3.5 to 5.0), low-normal. sections.heading: Proposed Procedure
sections.text:
Surgical aortic valve replacement, with concomitant single-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting to the left anterior descending artery, under cardiopulmonary bypass, is proposed within the next 4 to 6 weeks. The referring team has also asked what prehabilitation would be advised within that window.

An alternative under discussion is transcatheter aortic valve implantation, with staged or medical management of the coronary lesion instead. The key tension is this: the transcatheter approach avoids cardiopulmonary bypass, which would reduce peri-operative renal and pulmonary stress, but it leaves the coronary lesion to be managed separately and requires contrast exposure in a patient with a documented contrast allergy. Surgical replacement with bypass grafting treats both lesions in one operation but carries higher peri-operative risk to the kidneys and lungs in this patient.

sections.heading: Consultant Review
sections.text:
The consulting cardiologist's review states that severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with syncope and NYHA III symptoms means the natural history without intervention is poor, and conservative management is not considered a reasonable primary option. The coronary anatomy, a 70% proximal LAD stenosis, argues for definitive combined treatment, and on anatomy alone the surgical approach with bypass grafting is the most complete solution.

The cardiologist's recommendation is to proceed with surgical valve replacement and bypass grafting within 4 to 6 weeks, subject to council review. Renal function is flagged as the principal concern: the patient is chronic kidney disease stage 3b with diabetes and anaemia, and the predicted risk of post-operative acute kidney injury, including a non-trivial risk of temporary or permanent dialysis, is high with cardiopulmonary bypass. The patient's expressed fear of dialysis is noted as directly relevant to consent.

The cardiologist requests four things: formal nephrology input on peri-operative renal protection and dialysis-risk quantification; an anaesthesiology assessment of fitness given the COPD and frailty; explicit council consideration of the transcatheter approach as the lower-renal-stress alternative, noting the contrast allergy complicates its work-up and the coronary lesion would remain unaddressed; and a documented shared-decision conversation with the patient and his daughter before final consent.

— Dr. Meera Krishnan, Senior Consultant Cardiologist

ADMIN-KB-01.source_title: Informed consent and shared decision-making standards (synthetic summary)
ADMIN-KB-01.text: The standard of informed consent should be proportional to the risk of the procedure being proposed. For a procedure carrying a predicted mortality risk in the high-intermediate range, consent documentation should explicitly address that risk in terms the patient can understand, alongside the alternatives considered and why each was or was not recommended.

ADMIN-KB-04.source_title: Informed consent and shared decision-making standards (synthetic summary)
ADMIN-KB-04.text: Shared decision-making is not satisfied merely by a patient agreeing to proceed; it requires that the patient's own stated goals and concerns be weighed explicitly against the clinical recommendation, with any tension between the two acknowledged in the documented consent conversation rather than left unaddressed.

ADMIN-KB-05.source_title: Institutional protocol and resource checklist for high-risk procedures (synthetic summary)
ADMIN-KB-05.text: Any patient with a documented allergic reaction to contrast media requires a formal premedication protocol to be confirmed and recorded before any further contrast-requiring procedure or imaging study is scheduled, regardless of how the previous reaction was managed or how long ago it occurred, since the underlying sensitivity does not resolve with time.

ADMIN-KB-06.source_title: Institutional protocol and resource checklist for high-risk procedures (synthetic summary)
ADMIN-KB-06.text: Complex structural heart cases involving competing procedural options, such as a choice between surgical and transcatheter valve treatment, should be reviewed by a multidisciplinary heart team before a final recommendation is finalised, with the review and its conclusion documented in the patient's record.

ADMIN-KB-07.source_title: Institutional protocol and resource checklist for high-risk procedures (synthetic summary)
ADMIN-KB-07.text: Before scheduling a high-risk procedure with an elevated predicted risk of post-operative renal injury, confirmation of relevant institutional resources, including intensive care bed availability and renal replacement therapy capacity, should be documented as part of the pre-procedure checklist, not assumed to be available on the basis of general hospital capacity.

ANAES-KB-02.source_title: Anaesthetic fitness assessment for major cardiac surgery (synthetic summary)
ANAES-KB-02.text: Moderate COPD with reduced FEV1 increases the risk of prolonged mechanical ventilation and post-operative pulmonary complications after sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass. Pre-operative optimisation of bronchodilator therapy and a clear extubation plan are standard mitigations, and this risk alone is not generally considered a contraindication to proceeding with major cardiac surgery.

ANAES-KB-04.source_title: Anaesthetic fitness assessment for major cardiac surgery (synthetic summary)
ANAES-KB-04.text: Peri-operative risk assessment should weigh cumulative comorbidity burden rather than any single factor in isolation. A patient with three or more moderate-severity comorbidities, such as chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and respiratory disease together, generally carries materially higher anaesthetic risk than the sum of each condition's individually reported risk would suggest.

ANAES-KB-05.source_title: Peri-operative renal protection and dialysis readiness (synthetic summary)
ANAES-KB-05.text: Patients with chronic kidney disease stage 3b or worse undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass should have a documented renal-protection plan, including minimising bypass time where feasible, avoiding nephrotoxic agents peri-operatively, and close post-operative monitoring of creatinine and urine output for the first 48 to 72 hours.

ANAES-KB-06.source_title: Peri-operative renal protection and dialysis readiness (synthetic summary)
ANAES-KB-06.text: When the predicted risk of post-operative acute kidney injury is high, contingency planning should explicitly address dialysis readiness, including confirming access to renal replacement therapy and involving nephrology in the peri-operative period, rather than only after injury has already occurred.

ANAES-KB-07.source_title: Peri-operative renal protection and dialysis readiness (synthetic summary)
ANAES-KB-07.text: Pre-operative anaemia in a patient facing major cardiac surgery warrants a documented plan for blood management, since surgery of this kind carries a meaningful risk of further blood loss on top of an already reduced starting haemoglobin, and inadequate oxygen delivery peri-operatively can itself contribute to organ injury, including the kidneys.

CASE-allergies.text: Documented allergy to iodinated contrast media — a previous moderate reaction of urticaria and bronchospasm during a CT scan 5 years ago, managed without intensive care. A premedication protocol is required for any contrast exposure. No known drug allergies otherwise.

CASE-comorbidities.text:
1. Chronic kidney disease, stage 3b — baseline creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m², stable over the last 12 months; followed by nephrology; no prior dialysis.
2. Type 2 diabetes mellitus — 18 years, on oral agents; HbA1c 7.8%; background diabetic retinopathy; likely contributor to nephropathy.
3. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (moderate) — FEV1 55% predicted; one exacerbation requiring oral steroids in the past year; on inhaled bronchodilator therapy; no home oxygen.
4. Prior transient ischaemic attack — 3 years ago, full recovery; carotid Doppler shows 50% right internal carotid stenosis, asymptomatic since.
5. Hypertension — controlled on two agents.
6. Mild chronic anaemia — haemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, attributed to chronic kidney disease; iron studies borderline.
7. Borderline frailty — Clinical Frailty Scale 4 to 5 (vulnerable to mildly frail); gait speed 0.7 m/s, which is slow; hand-grip strength below age norm; unintentional weight loss as noted in the patient profile. Cognition is intact, MoCA 26 out of 30. Mood is mildly anxious about surgery, with no depression.

CASE-consultant-review.text:
The consulting cardiologist's review states that severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with syncope and NYHA III symptoms means the natural history without intervention is poor, and conservative management is not considered a reasonable primary option. The coronary anatomy, a 70% proximal LAD stenosis, argues for definitive combined treatment, and on anatomy alone the surgical approach with bypass grafting is the most complete solution.

The cardiologist's recommendation is to proceed with surgical valve replacement and bypass grafting within 4 to 6 weeks, subject to council review. Renal function is flagged as the principal concern: the patient is chronic kidney disease stage 3b with diabetes and anaemia, and the predicted risk of post-operative acute kidney injury, including a non-trivial risk of temporary or permanent dialysis, is high with cardiopulmonary bypass. The patient's expressed fear of dialysis is noted as directly relevant to consent.

The cardiologist requests four things: formal nephrology input on peri-operative renal protection and dialysis-risk quantification; an anaesthesiology assessment of fitness given the COPD and frailty; explicit council consideration of the transcatheter approach as the lower-renal-stress alternative, noting the contrast allergy complicates its work-up and the coronary lesion would remain unaddressed; and a documented shared-decision conversation with the patient and his daughter before final consent.

— Dr. Meera Krishnan, Senior Consultant Cardiologist

CASE-diagnoses.text:
The patient presented to the cardiology outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness, now NYHA Class III (symptomatic walking approximately 100 metres or one flight of stairs), two episodes of exertional chest tightness, and one witnessed syncopal episode three weeks ago while climbing stairs, resulting in a minor fall without fracture.

Evaluation has confirmed severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with concomitant single-vessel coronary artery disease. The syncopal episode and worsening functional class indicate the disease has entered a high-risk symptomatic phase. Without intervention, symptomatic severe aortic stenosis of this profile carries a substantially elevated 1 to 2 year mortality risk.

CASE-procedure.text:
Surgical aortic valve replacement, with concomitant single-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting to the left anterior descending artery, under cardiopulmonary bypass, is proposed within the next 4 to 6 weeks. The referring team has also asked what prehabilitation would be advised within that window.

An alternative under discussion is transcatheter aortic valve implantation, with staged or medical management of the coronary lesion instead. The key tension is this: the transcatheter approach avoids cardiopulmonary bypass, which would reduce peri-operative renal and pulmonary stress, but it leaves the coronary lesion to be managed separately and requires contrast exposure in a patient with a documented contrast allergy. Surgical replacement with bypass grafting treats both lesions in one operation but carries higher peri-operative risk to the kidneys and lungs in this patient.

CASE-profile.text:
The patient is a 76-year-old man, height 168 cm, weight 61 kg (BMI 21.6), with an unintentional weight loss of approximately 5 kg over the past 8 months. He lives with his spouse; his daughter, who lives nearby, is the primary family contact. He is independent for basic activities but needs assistance with shopping and stairs. He is a retired school teacher. He is an ex-smoker (30 pack-years, quit 12 years ago) and does not drink alcohol.

The patient has stated: "I want to be able to walk to the temple again and see my granddaughter's wedding next year. I will accept surgery if the doctors believe it is the right thing, but I am afraid of ending up on dialysis." His daughter has expressed concern about surgical risk and has asked whether "the valve can be fixed without open surgery."

CASE-tests.text:
Laboratory results, 10 July: creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (reference 0.7 to 1.3), stable over 12 months. eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73m² (reference above 90), consistent with chronic kidney disease stage 3b. Urea 58 mg/dL (reference 15 to 40), elevated. Potassium 4.9 mmol/L (reference 3.5 to 5.1), upper normal. Haemoglobin 10.8 g/dL (reference 13 to 17), mild anaemia. HbA1c 7.8% (reference below 6.5), suboptimal control. NT-proBNP 2450 pg/mL (reference below 300), significantly elevated. Albumin 3.4 g/dL (reference 3.5 to 5.0), low-normal. INR 1.0, platelets 190000 — no coagulopathy.

Transthoracic echocardiogram, 8 July: severe calcific aortic stenosis, valve area 0.7 cm², mean gradient 46 mmHg, peak velocity 4.4 m/s. Left ventricular ejection fraction 45%, a mild-to-moderate impairment, with moderate LV hypertrophy. Mild mitral regurgitation; mild pulmonary hypertension, estimated PASP 42 mmHg.

Coronary angiography, 11 July, minimal-contrast protocol with premedication: 70% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with other vessels showing only minor irregularities. The procedure was tolerated; creatinine 48 hours after the procedure was 2.0 mg/dL, returning to baseline by day 5.

Pulmonary function tests: FEV1 55% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.62, a moderate obstructive pattern indicating adequate but reduced respiratory reserve for major surgery.

Risk scores calculated by the cardiology team: STS predicted risk of mortality for SAVR with CABG is approximately 6.8%, a high-intermediate surgical risk. EuroSCORE II is approximately 7.5%. The predicted risk of post-operative acute kidney injury is judged high, given chronic kidney disease stage 3b, diabetes, anaemia, and the anticipated cardiopulmonary bypass time.

PHYS-KB-02.source_title: Natural history and risk markers of severe aortic stenosis (synthetic summary)
PHYS-KB-02.text: A syncopal episode in the setting of severe aortic stenosis is considered a high-risk marker, reflecting the heart's reduced ability to increase output during exertion. Its occurrence typically accelerates the timeline for considering intervention, since the risk of a subsequent, potentially fatal event rises once syncope has occurred.

PHYS-KB-04.source_title: Natural history and risk markers of severe aortic stenosis (synthetic summary)
PHYS-KB-04.text: NYHA functional class III indicates symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity, such as breathlessness after walking a short distance or climbing one flight of stairs. This class of limitation, in the context of a structural cardiac lesion, is generally regarded as a threshold beyond which conservative management alone is unlikely to be adequate.

PHYS-KB-07.source_title: Interacting comorbidities in cardiac risk assessment (synthetic summary)
PHYS-KB-07.text: There is no established medical therapy that reverses severe calcific aortic stenosis; guideline-directed medical management in this setting is limited to treating associated conditions, such as hypertension or heart failure symptoms, rather than the valve lesion itself. Definitive treatment requires either surgical or transcatheter valve intervention.

SURG-KB-01.source_title: Surgical risk stratification for valve and coronary procedures (synthetic summary)
SURG-KB-01.text: A composite predicted mortality risk of 4% to 8% on validated cardiac surgical risk models is generally classified as high-intermediate risk. Patients in this band are not routinely excluded from surgery, but the risk-benefit balance depends heavily on modifiable factors such as renal function, frailty, and respiratory reserve, and typically warrants multidisciplinary heart-team review before a final decision.

SURG-KB-02.source_title: Surgical risk stratification for valve and coronary procedures (synthetic summary)
SURG-KB-02.text: Cardiopulmonary bypass exposes the kidneys to reduced perfusion pressure and a systemic inflammatory response, both of which can precipitate acute kidney injury. Baseline chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and anaemia each independently raise this risk, and their combination is additive rather than simply cumulative, meaning a patient with all three faces materially higher risk than any single factor alone would suggest.

SURG-KB-04.source_title: Surgical risk stratification for valve and coronary procedures (synthetic summary)
SURG-KB-04.text: Moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with FEV1 in the 50 to 60 percent predicted range is associated with a measurably higher risk of prolonged ventilation and pulmonary complications after sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass, compared with normal lung function. This risk is generally considered manageable with pre-operative optimisation and is not, on its own, a reason to decline surgery.

SURG-KB-07.source_title: Aortic valve intervention options and coronary revascularisation strategy (synthetic summary)
SURG-KB-07.text: When severe aortic stenosis coexists with significant proximal coronary disease, concurrent surgical treatment of both lesions in a single operation is generally preferred over a staged approach, because it avoids a second procedure and its associated risk, provided the patient's overall risk profile tolerates the combined operation.

SURG-KB-08.source_title: Aortic valve intervention options and coronary revascularisation strategy (synthetic summary)
SURG-KB-08.text: An aortic valve area below 1.0 cm squared with a mean gradient above 40 mmHg defines severe aortic stenosis. Once a patient with severe stenosis becomes symptomatic, expert consensus favours intervention over continued observation, since symptom onset itself marks a significant worsening in prognosis regardless of the specific values recorded.
